metadata.title: Why Flights Are Late
metadata.section: Section F: Logistics, Infrastructure & Public Health
metadata.data_notes: Percent of all scheduled flights that arrived late for each cause (national, all airlines).

events.label: Airline meltdown: carrier delays peak at 9.2%

explanation.summary: Why are flights late? This chart shows the share of all US airline flights that arrived late because of each cause. The biggest cause today is a domino effect: a plane arrives late because it was already late on its previous trip.
explanation.methodology: Monthly on-time data for all reporting US airlines from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (Airline Service Quality Performance, Form 234), read from the BTS delay-cause tables. Each value is the percent of all scheduled flights that arrived 15+ minutes late because of that cause. "Weather" covers only extreme weather; ordinary weather delays are counted under the air traffic system (NAS).

key_findings.title: December 2007: The Worst Month
key_findings.description: 31.8% of all flights arrived late, the highest on the chart. Air traffic system delays alone affected 10.4% of flights.
key_findings.significance: Crowded skies before the recession made delays routine.

key_findings.title: December 2022: Airline Meltdowns
key_findings.description: Delays caused by the airlines themselves (crews, maintenance, scheduling) reached 9.2% of flights, the highest on the chart, as a winter storm broke airline crew systems.
key_findings.significance: After the pandemic, airlines had too few staff to recover from disruptions.

key_findings.title: July 2024: The Domino Record
key_findings.description: Late-arriving aircraft delayed 11.4% of all flights, the highest on the chart. In 2025, about 21.6% of flights arrived late on average, up from 16.5% in 2012.
key_findings.significance: Tight schedules mean one late plane delays many flights after it.
